title: After hours jam spots and working two jobs a night
summary: She and Willard list after-hours places such as Lovejoy's, Backstage and the Brown House, and describe musicians working two jobs a night.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Now, a little later, when they did get into the jam session thing they used to go to the -- there was the Apex and there was Lovejoy's and there was another place -- of course Ivy Anderson, Ivy had a chicken place.
They didn't have music there, did they?

They didn't have music, no, no. But there was another place. I can't even -- I can't think -- isn't that funny, I can't think of the name of that place now. But this was a very popular place there. They used to have jam -- the guys would go there and jam, you know, after hours.
Then they began to open up all over town, you know.
Yes.
Everybody then got the idea of going into that, because the musicians loved to have someplace to go. When they got off from work they liked to unwind, you know.
Uh-huh.
And this was a way of unwinding.
Lovejoy's was upstairs at Vernon and
Central.
Right.
And then I guess it was a little later on that Stuff Crouch had the Backstage.
Right.
A little down Vernon, a few doors.
Right.
Down Vernon and just east of Central.
Uh-huh.
And -- well, I don't know about any other -- I'm sure there were other after hours places on the avenue.

There were other places. There was a place down at 54th and Central Avenue, and that was called -- oh, Brown's, the Brown House, or something we called it. The Browns, Mr. and Mrs. Brown ran that place. That was quite a place, and they had very good entertainment. They had a regular group that played there, and as I say, people used to jam and sing. Vocalists -- people used to love to go there because they could sing, you know. They'd get a chance to sing along with these good groups.
Was that before or after hours, or both?
After hours.
That was after hours.
After hours, yeah. But all of the
musicians worked, they worked two jobs, most of them worked two jobs, you know.
Uh-huh.

They'd work the first club -- and at that time there was no such thing as going to work at 9:00 o'clock. You went to work at 8:00 o'clock. You worked from 8:00 until 2:00, and then at 2:00 o'clock -- maybe you'd stop at about 10 minutes, at a quarter to 2:00 or something like that, give them a chance to clear the joint out, you know, and then you'd be on your way to your next gig, see?
Uh-huh.

To the regular breakfast club there. And all of these places were just packed nightly. And you had the best chicken in the world, you know, biscuits, honey. Oh, it was something. And you'd get a chance to see your friends, you know. This is the thing that we miss today. You just don't get a chance to see people unless people -- now we get a chance to see each other -- we don't see each other until somebody dies.
Yeah.

At a funeral, you know, we get a chance to see everybody. Well, you used to keep up with everybody. And another thing -- of course I'm getting a little ahead of myself again, but you know, I married shortly after I came to California, for the second time, and my son Talmadge
